ARGUMENT
A. Mr. Holland's Rule II Submission raises substantial federal
Constitutional Claims that Warrant this Court's Consideration and
Present a Substantial Possibility of Success on the Merits
Mr. Holland contends that the Third Circuit's refusal to permit him
to discharge his appointed appellate counsel and proceed pro se after
counsel filed an opening brief without giving Mr. Holland an opportunity
to review the brief implicates 'his due process rights, fundamental fairness,
28 U.S.C. SS 1654, and ineffective assistance of counsel. Where a defendant
wishes to proceed pro se, courts. must give effect to that choice unless it
is clearly and unequivocally contrary to the defendant's interest and made
knowingly and intelligently after proper admonitions. The question
whether the Third Circuit's denial was consistent with controlling precedents
is a federal question of first impression for this court to review via
Mr. Holland's Rule 11 submission.
The issues raised impåidate the proper allocation of authority between
an indigent criminal appellant and appointed appellate counsel over the
the conduct of appellate litigation (See Jones v. Barnes, 463 U.S. 745
(1983) addressing counsel's discretion to winnow issues on appeal)), and
the proper assessment of ineffective assistant of counsel or the break-down
of the attorney-client relationship (see Strickland v. Washington, 466
U.S. 668 (1984)). Mr. Holland respectfully submits that the dissents in
JoneS • (Justice Brennan's dissent) and Strickland (Justice Marshall's
dissent) articulate concerns that are directly relevant to Mr. Holland 's
circumstances and merit this Court's review in the present case to protect
rights of criminal appellatnt's who wish to control their appeals.
The Third Ciruit also misinterpreted therSupreme Courts decision

ensuring that criminal appellants' constitutional rights to counsel, to
waive counsel, and to meaningful appellate review are respected and adjudicated
carefully. Allowing the Third Circuit to proceed before this Court rules

€0 ES CCW
I hope you are doing well. You should have received the initial brief and all five
volumes of the appendix.
I have reviewed your recent filings in the Third Circuit Court of Appeals —
specifically, (1) your motion to have your pro se supplemental brief considered and (2)
your pro se supplemental brief. The Third Circuit denied your motion on November 5,
2025. You should have received a copy of the Order directly from the Third Circuit, but I
have enclosed a copy as well.
In light of your motion and the Court's denial, I want to reiterate your options. As
we have discussed, the Third Circuit will not consider pro se submissions when an
appellant is represented by counsel. This is the Circuit's standard procedure, as
explained in United States v. Turner, 677 F.3d 570 (3d Cir. 2012) (except in cases
governed by Anders, parties represented by counsel may not file pro se briefs). The
Court cited the Turner case in its Order, and I have enclosed a copy.
In your case, therefore, the Court will not consider your pro se supplemental
brief as long as we represent you and did not file an Anders brief. If you want the Court
to consider your supplemental brief and/or any issues not raised in the brief we filed,
you must file a motion to waive counsel. You must state that you are aware of the risks
of proceeding pro se and that you still wish to proceed pro se. If that motion is granted,
the Court will advise you as to how to proceed.
